verdict.summary: There is no app-review or listing step for standard OAuth 2.0 apps in the sources we found. Once you have a developer account and a configured App, any X user can authorize it. The real hurdles are paying for usage (pay-per-use credits, loaded up front), X's automation and AI-reply rules, and a risk of suspension. Composio has no managed X app, so you have to register your own.
verdict.approval_wait: None reported for standard use cases. AI and bot use cases reportedly get an extra manual review, and no timeline is published. AI reply bots need X's prior written approval.

gates.name: Self-serve developer account + App
gates.unlocks: You create a Project and App in the Developer Console and connect your own X account through Composio.
limits: One developer account per person. An individual account can't be converted into a team account.
Up to 10 Apps per developer account by default.
Pay-per-use: you need a payment method and loaded credits before API calls work (reported by a secondary source).
Access tokens expire after 2 hours unless you request offline.access.

gates.name: Other X users authorize your App (no allowlist mode found)
gates.unlocks: Invited or test users can authorize the App. The sources describe no test-user allowlist or sandbox mode: once OAuth 2.0 is enabled, any X user who opens your authorize link can connect.
limits: Every call is billed to your credits at pay-per-use rates (reported: about $0.005 per post read and $0.015 per post created).
The App description is shown publicly on the Sign in with X consent flow.
Tweet and user lookup are limited to 900 requests per 15 minutes per App under OAuth 2.0.

gates.name: Production (pay-per-use, public)
gates.unlocks: Anyone can connect. No marketplace or listing review was found for standard OAuth apps. Free 'Public Utility' access and Enterprise are separate, manually reviewed routes.
limits: Reported cap of 3 million post reads per billing cycle on pay-per-use. Above that you need Enterprise, which starts at about $42K/month.
Operating an AI reply bot needs X's prior written approval. Self-serve replies are accepted only when the original author mentioned or quoted your account.
Automated accounts must turn on the 'Automated' profile label.
Free Public Utility access is decided by manual, case-by-case review, and apps have been reclassified to paid without notice.
gates.time_to_reach: Immediate for standard use cases. AI and bot use cases reportedly get an extra review with an unknown timeline.

steps.title: Prepare the X account that will own the App
steps.detail: Log in to the X account that should own the developer account. Verify its email (and phone if asked) and check that it's in good standing. The email on the account at submission is used for all application correspondence and can't be changed afterwards.
gotchas: Use a long-lived team or company account. One developer account per person, and an individual account can't become a team account.
Any existing apps on this account must also be in good standing.

steps.title: Sign up for a developer account at console.x.com
steps.detail: Go to console.x.com, sign up and accept the Developer Agreement. Describe your use case honestly. Secondary sources say standard use cases are approved automatically, while AI and bot use cases get an extra review.
gotchas: Requests rejected for compliance reasons can't be reopened, so describe automation and AI use accurately on the first try.
The Developer Agreement, Developer Policy and Automation Rules apply to every app type, not only bots.

steps.title: Add a payment method and load credits
steps.detail: Under X's pay-per-use model, you buy credits up front in the Developer Console. A secondary source says you can't make calls until a payment method is added and credits are loaded. Check current prices in the console, because the support page still lists the old Free/Basic/Pro tiers.
gotchas: Reported prices: about $0.015 per post created, $0.20 per post containing a URL, and $0.005 per post read.
Free scaled access is kept only for approved 'Public Utility' apps, decided by manual review.

steps.title: Create a Project and an App
steps.detail: In the Developer Console, create a Project, then create an App inside it. An App must belong to a Project to call X API v2 endpoints, and the Project carries the access level and monthly cap.
gotchas: Accounts are limited to 10 Apps by default. Getting more requires a request through the API policy support form, with a use case for each App.

steps.title: Enable OAuth 2.0 and register the callback URL
steps.detail: Open the App's authentication settings and turn on OAuth 2.0. Set the App type to 'Web App' (a confidential client that gets a Client Secret). Then add the Composio callback URL exactly as Composio shows it.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: X requires an exact match on the callback URL. Even a trailing slash or a v1/v3 path difference will break the flow.
Composio's default redirect URI and the path seen in a probe differed (/api/v1/auth-apps/add vs /api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback). Copy the one shown in your auth config.

steps.title: Write the App description
steps.detail: Draft a short, accurate App description. It becomes public when users go through Sign in with X, so it effectively serves as your consent-screen text.

steps.title: Copy the Client ID and Client Secret
steps.detail: In the Developer Console, copy the value under the 'Client ID' header and the Client Secret, which Web App and Automated App/bot types receive. Store them in a secrets manager.
gotchas: Native App and Single page App types are public clients and get no secret. Use Web App for a server-side integration like Composio.

steps.title: Choose a minimal scope list
steps.detail: Composio's default list for X is broad, covering DMs, mutes, blocks, lists, bookmarks and more. Map the tools your agent actually uses to X scopes and request only those. Include offline.access so tokens can be refreshed.

values.label: Suggested minimum scopes
values.value: tweet.read users.read offline.access (add tweet.write, media.write, etc. only if used)

gotchas: Secondary sources say likes and follows were removed from self-serve access in 2026. Check those scopes against the current changelog before relying on them.
Without offline.access, tokens expire after 2 hours and you get no refresh token.

steps.title: Create a Composio auth config with your own credentials
steps.detail: In Composio, create an auth config for the 'twitter' toolkit using your own OAuth 2.0 credentials (Client ID and Client Secret) and your trimmed scope list. Composio doesn't offer managed OAuth for X, so this step is required.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

steps.title: Run a test authorization with your own account
steps.detail: Start a connection through Composio, log in to X, approve the consent screen, then make one cheap read call such as looking up your own user. X checks the client_id only after login, so a wrong Client ID shows up at the consent step, not on the first request.
gotchas: The authorization code expires 30 seconds after it's issued. Slow manual code exchanges will fail.
The flow uses PKCE (S256 or plain) plus a state value. Composio handles this, but custom clients must too.
X publishes no OIDC discovery document, so take endpoints from the docs.

steps.title: Configure automation compliance before going live
steps.detail: If the agent posts, replies or interacts on users' behalf, turn on the 'Automated' profile label on the bot account. Make sure replies are sent only when the original author mentioned or quoted your account. If you run an AI reply bot, get X's written approval first.
steps.est_time: 15-30 min (plus approval time if you run an AI reply bot)
gotchas: Auto-replying to keywords or trends is prohibited, as is scraping or browser automation outside the API.
Violations can suspend the App, and suspended apps have not been restored automatically even after the owning account was reinstated.

steps.title: Monitor credits, caps and App health
steps.detail: Track credit balance and monthly usage in the Developer Console, because X's two documentation sites state monthly caps differently. Keep the App in active use to avoid an inactivity suspension.
gotchas: Reported cap of 3 million post reads per billing cycle on pay-per-use. Beyond that you need Enterprise (from about $42K/month).

requirements.item: X account with verified email, in good standing
requirements.detail: Phone verification may also be needed. The email can't be changed after the application is submitted.
Accepted at sign-up. Its rules and the Automation Rules apply to every app type.
Pay-per-use with no subscription. A secondary source says calls are blocked until credits are loaded.

requirements.item: App inside a Project with OAuth 2.0 enabled
requirements.detail: Web App type gives you a Client Secret. The callback URL must match exactly.
Shown publicly during Sign in with X.

requirements.item: 'Automated' profile label for accounts that post or reply automatically
requirements.detail: Required by X's developer guidelines for apps that post, reply or interact on behalf of users.

requirements.item: Written approval from X for AI reply bots
requirements.detail: Reported by a secondary source quoting X policy.

scopes.effect: Without it, access tokens last 2 hours and no refresh token is issued. Include it for any long-running agent.
Basic read access. No per-scope review flag in X's scope table. Reads are billed per post.

No per-scope review flag found, but posting brings in the automation rules: the Automated label, reply restrictions, and written approval for AI reply bots. Posts cost more, especially ones with URLs.
Separate from users.read. Request it only if you need the user's email address. No review flag found.
Included in Composio's defaults, but secondary sources say likes and follows were removed from self-serve access in 2026. They may not work on pay-per-use.
Included in Composio's defaults. Self-serve availability couldn't be confirmed from official pages. Requesting them widens the consent screen.

blockers.cause: Rejected for compliance reasons, for example a misdescribed or prohibited use case.
blockers.fix: Describe the use case accurately up front. Compliance rejections can't be reopened.

blockers.cause: AI and bot use cases reportedly trigger an additional manual review.
blockers.fix: Expect a delay, and explain clearly how the automation follows the Automation Rules.

blockers.symptom: Callback or redirect_uri error during authorization
blockers.cause: The callback URL registered on the X App doesn't exactly match the one Composio sends.
blockers.fix: Copy the exact callback URL from your Composio auth config into the App's OAuth 2.0 settings.

blockers.symptom: Code exchange fails with invalid or expired code
blockers.cause: The authorization code is valid for only 30 seconds.
blockers.fix: Exchange the code immediately. Composio does this automatically.

blockers.symptom: API calls fail after a successful connection
blockers.cause: No payment method or credits loaded on the pay-per-use account.
blockers.fix: Load credits in the Developer Console.

blockers.symptom: "This App has violated X Rules and policies. As a result, certain functions will be limited."
blockers.cause: Automation or policy violation, such as keyword auto-replies, an unapproved AI reply bot or a missing Automated label.
blockers.fix: Fix the behavior and request reinstatement through developer support. Suspended apps aren't restored automatically.

blockers.cause: The App hasn't been used for a long time.
blockers.fix: Keep the App active, or contact support to reinstate it.

blockers.symptom: A free Public Utility app is suddenly billed as pay-per-use
blockers.cause: X has reclassified Public Utility apps without notice.
blockers.fix: Post on the developer forum to request a staff review. Some apps have been restored this way.

composio.note: Composio has no managed OAuth app for X, so you have to bring your own from day one. That means a Client ID and Client Secret from a Web App-type X App, with Composio's callback URL registered exactly on that App. Composio's default redirect URI (backend.composio.dev/api/v1/auth-apps/add) differs from the v3 callback path seen in testing, so paste whatever your auth config displays. Composio's default scope list is very broad. Cut it to what your tools use, keep offline.access, and note that like and follow scopes may no longer work for self-serve.

open_questions: No test-user allowlist or sandbox mode, and no public listing or app review (privacy policy, logo, demo video, domain verification, security assessment) appeared in any source. Treat these as unknown, not confirmed absent.
No official timeline for developer-account approval was found. 'Automated for standard use, extra review for AI/bot use' comes from a secondary blog.
Which Composio callback to register: /api/v1/auth-apps/add or /api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback. Use what your Composio auth config shows.
Official docs conflict on monthly caps and on whether new developers get any free tier. Check pricing and caps on console.x.com.
The Developer Console sits behind a login wall, so exact App creation form fields and labels weren't observed directly.
Self-serve availability of the DM, follow and like scopes couldn't be confirmed from official pages.
The Public Utility application route (Government end-user request form) comes from a forum staff reply, not an official policy page.
Enterprise approval steps and timelines weren't verified.
